newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong must live with China legislature - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong must live with China legislature - analysts.

text.p: China's newly selected legislature for Hong Kong is a reality that the people of the British territory must accept, whatever the doubts over its legality, analysts and commentators said on Sunday.
A century and a half of British rule ends for the 6.3 million residents of Hong Kong at midnight on June 30, when London hands back the territory to Beijing.

A committee handpicked from Hong Kong's business and political elite cast votes in red envelopes in the city hall of the Chinese city of Shenzhen on Saturday to name the 60 people who will make up the territory's post-handover legislature.

At issue is whether the 400-member Selection Committee and the legislature-in-waiting it picked has a mandate to replace the colony's Legislative Council, elected last year by more than one million Hong Kong voters.
Beijing has vowed to scrap the elected legislature since colonial Governor Chris Patten introduced a series of political reforms enlarging the franchise in 1992.

China's Xinhua news agency hailed the creation of the new body, which includes 33 incumbent legislators among its stocking of pro-Beijing politicians and businesspeople, as an "important guarantee for the smooth transition of Hong Kong".

Hong Kong University law professor Nihal Jayawickrama said the selection process was "wholly lacking in legitimacy" but added that Beijing's vow to replace the current legislature meant changes for Hong Kong after the handover.
"Despite all the protestations about the existing legal and judicial system remaining in force, the fact is it's not going to remain in force -- it's going to change," he said.

The legality of the interim legislature has been questioned by pro-democracy groups in Hong Kong as well as British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind, who challenged China to seek a ruling on the body at the International Court of Justice in The Hague.
But any action by the world court would require Beijing's co-signature to proceed, and comments from Chinese officials make this unlikely.

Pro-China newspapers in Hong Kong echoed the words of Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen by saying on Sunday that the territory's colonial government should accept the outcome and cooperate with the new Provisional Legislative Council.
Ta Kung Pao said Saturday's selection process, like that of post-colonial leader-in-waiting Tung Chee-hwa on December 11, was "an extremely successful democratic election".
"The basic essence of democracy is that people are masters of their own house," the newspaper said.
While the question of legality lingered, the South China Morning Post newspaper said, the tide was turning against Patten, who has angered China with a series of political reforms since 1992.

"Though Mr Patten remains in Government House for another six months, the balance of power is tilting ever more strongly against him, towards Beijing and those who will claim their legitimacy from the changes July 1 will bring," it said.
Speaking on British Broadcasting Corp (BBC) radio on Saturday, Patten said China's move would "throw question marks over the early months of the government of Hong Kong after July".
"Here we are having foisted on us institutions which, frankly, you wouldn't try to run a tennis club with," he said.
Despite criticism of the selection before Saturday, London and Washington had little to say after the votes had been tallied in Shenzhen.
The Foreign Office said Britain had little to add to Rifkind's remarks, while a U.S. State Department spokeswoman said the department had no comment.
Martin Lee, the leader of the Democratic Party -- Hong Kong's largest -- has vowed to seek a court injunction against the provisional body if it meets in Hong Kong before July 1.
"If this sham legislature is lawful, why not appoint it and have it meet in Hong Kong, where the Supreme Court can decide on its legality?" Lee said on Friday.
But the voice of Hong Kong's pro-democracy camp appeared to be fading on Saturday when a march to protest against the Selection Committee attracted only 200 demonstrators.
